title: Lover, beloved, love
hookLine: Augustine's picture of the Trinity from human love

lines: THE ONE LOVING, THE ONE LOVED.
cards: A grandmother kneels in a hallway, teaching a small boy to tie his shoe. Loop, swoop, pull. He gets it wrong, she laughs, and they start again.
Count what's in that hallway. Her, the one loving. Him, the one being loved.
And something else, not a third person exactly, but real enough that anyone walking past would see it: the love itself, running between them.
Augustine, the same restless bishop from yesterday, wrote a long book on the Trinity, the teaching you first met in year one. Partway through, he stops at this very thing: love.

teach.b: His starting point is a short line in the first letter of John: "for God is love." Augustine takes it seriously. If God is love, what does love need?
Someone who loves. Someone who is loved. And the love itself.
Lover, beloved, love: three, and yet one thing happening. In his book on the Trinity, he says that if you see love, you see the Trinity.
Some readers map it this way: the Father as the one who loves, the Son as the one loved, the Spirit as the love that binds them; Augustine himself ties the Spirit closely to love.
In John's Gospel, Jesus prays to the Father: "thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world." Love between the Father and the Son, older than the world. Here's what's honest about Augustine.
He doesn't call the picture done.

He says it's a beginning, a place to rest a moment, and keeps climbing. He turns inward, to the human mind: the mind, its knowing of itself, its love of itself. Later he tries memory, understanding and will.
And near the end of the book he admits that every picture he's tried falls short of God. Christians weigh these images differently.
Western theologians have drawn on them; some Orthodox theologians prefer to begin where the Cappadocians did, from the three persons. Augustine never claimed his picture was the whole thing.
He offered it as a window, small and human: love needs more than one to be love.

how: Christians speak of the Trinity as the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, one God, and some preachers and teachers in the Western churches use Augustine's picture of lover, beloved and love to describe it.

o: in Augustine's picture, the one who loves
a romantic partner, as in a love song
the one who receives love and gives none back

s: Augustine said his lover, beloved, love picture explains the Trinity completely
he called it a beginning, kept climbing, and admitted every picture falls short of God.
Augustine starts from the line God is love
"for God is love," from the first letter of John.
after the picture of love, Augustine turns inward to the human mind
he tries the mind, its knowing and its love, then memory, understanding and will.

games.q: you're Augustine. you've found a picture of the Trinity in love: lover, beloved, love. it's beautiful. what do you do next?
o: stop there. the picture is complete.
call it a beginning, and keep looking for better ones.
games.why: he rests there for a moment, then turns inward to the mind, and near the end of the book admits every picture falls short.

practice: Bring to mind two people you've seen love each other well: a parent and a child, a couple at a bus stop, two old friends laughing at the same joke one more time.
Notice the one giving, the one receiving, and then the thing between them that belongs to neither alone, and stay with that third thing. If you pray, you can thank God for it.

wordCard.voice: Lover. In Augustine's picture of the Trinity, love needs three things to be love: the one who loves, the one who is loved, and the love itself.
